results.title: LSR, Astha Kunj And The Unfinished Fight For Women's Right To Public Spaces
results.article: Last year, five young women from the **Cities for Youth Programme** in Ajmer started Apno Thiyo, pop-up chai stops to create safe spaces for women. In Delhi, after a 17-year-old was gang-raped at Astha Kunj Park, Lady Shri Ram College shut down temporarily while highlighting poor park maintenance and non-operational CCTV cameras. **Safetipin**'s Kalpana Viswanath emphasizes addressing infrastructure issues rather than protectionist measures. Initiatives like Why Loiter? promote women's right to public spaces, with free transport in Karnataka showing increased employment for women.

results.title: Allahabad High Court bans hookah in Indian restaurants, cafes
results.article: On Tuesday, the **Allahabad High Court** ruled that restaurants and cafes in India cannot serve hookah to customers even in designated smoking areas. Justices Shekhar B Saraf and A K Chaudhary dismissed petitions seeking permission for serving hookah under valid licences, stating it violates Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products Act, 2003, and Prohibition of Smoking Rules, 2008. The court emphasized that operating a hookah involves providing a service and not just renting equipment, rejecting arguments made by petitioners. It clarified that the Food Safety Department cannot issue licences for hookah bars and directed police to ensure compliance with statutory restrictions. The judgement prioritized non-smokers' right to clean air over business interests.

results.title: Keralam needs 27 GW renewable capacity to reach 100% goal by 2040
results.article:
A study by **WRI India** released in **Thiruvananthapuram** on September 29, 2026, states **Keralam** needs 27 GW of renewable capacity to reach a 100% RE-based goal by 2040. The report, presented at a **Kerala State Electricity Board** workshop, estimates a ₹64,890 crore cost. It suggests private and international finance are essential as current thermal power meets 60% of demand.
Becoming a fully renewable energy (RE)-based State by 2040 could prove a “challenging” task for Keralam, indicates a new study released in Thiruvananthapuram on Tuesday (September 29, 2026). The southern State would need at least 27 gigawatts (GW) of renewable capacity addition to meet the 2040 demand “purely from renewables, hydro and nuclear without any thermal power support,” according to an ‘exploratory’ Zero Thermal 2040 scenario considered in ‘Pathways for Kerala’s Clean Energy Transition,’ a study conducted by WRI India. Financial implications The estimated financial input needed for a complete shift from a thermal power-dominant landscape to a fully RE-based one is huge. The report, released at a workshop organised by the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) and WRI India, pegs the estimate at ₹64,890 crore, 96% higher than in a business-as-usual scenario. While Keralam aspires to become 100% RE-based by 2040 and carbon neutral by 2050, around 60% of its electricity demand is being met by thermal power plants located in other States. “By contrast, the share of RE (wind, solar and small hydro) stood at 7%, with large hydro and nuclear contributing the remaining share,” the report observed. Private participation It has recommended a multi-pronged strategy that combines rapid deployment of diverse RE technologies, long-term renewable power purchase agreements with out-of-State generators, and adoption of decentralised RE solutions for a potential 100% RE transition by 2040. For such a transition, Keralam may need to tap private and international finance. “Larger private participation in the distribution sector is essential, along with strengthened consumer participation in Keralam’s energy governance,” according to the report. Three scenarios Meant to brief stakeholders on possible pathways that Keralam can take, the study considers three scenarios other than the one where the State moves away completely from thermal sources. results.title: Elephants Quickly Adapt Tactics to Get Food, Study Finds
results.article: In a study published in PLOS One on September 9, 2026, **Sydney Hope** and colleagues at Hunter College tested Asian elephants' ability to adjust their behavior when familiar methods failed. At Thailand's National Elephant Institute, they observed that elephants could abandon old habits and find new ways to reach food within seconds after researchers rotated the box opening. Older elephants took longer to adapt, suggesting age-related cognitive decline. The study highlights potential applications for conservation efforts aimed at reducing human-elephant conflicts.
